title: Your inner republic
intro: In the Republic Plato describes five regimes, from the rule of wisdom down to tyranny, and shows each one growing out of a kind of soul. Athena calls this psycho-politics (ψυχοπολιτική): the polis mirrors the soul, so 'the first polity we must learn to govern is our soul'. This reflection looks at what actually rules your decisions: wisdom, honour, money and security, every passing wish, or one desire above all. It is a mirror, not a test.

types.name: Aristocracy: wisdom governs
types.about: In Plato's best regime the wise part governs, the spirited part is its ally, and the desires keep their place; in you, choices mostly come from what you have understood to be good. Athena reads this as justice in its inner sense, τὰ ἑαυτοῦ πράττειν: each part of the soul doing its own around the one fiery Self, the soul's own constitution (πολίτευμα). Athena also warns that a constitution of the soul built only from mind and heart, with no vital force behind it, has no foundation: wisdom rules, and it needs will and strength to guard it.

types.name: Timocracy: honour governs
types.short: The love of honour and winning
types.about: Honour governs: recognition, standing, winning, being seen to do well. In Plato's second regime the spirited part (τὸ θυμοειδές) takes the throne, and the timocratic person is ambitious and competitive, a lover of honour and of victory. Athena equates the spirited part with the heart and the emotions, and its fire is real; yet in the cave the honours and prizes handed out for predicting shadows lose all their value once the source is seen.

types.name: Oligarchy: money and security govern
types.about: Money and security govern: saving, insuring, keeping, the fear of not having enough. In Plato's third regime the money-loving part is set on the throne as a great king within, and the oligarchic person holds the other desires down out of fear rather than understanding. Athena's reading goes to the root: the soul seeks a fullness that money cannot give ('however much we are paid, money cannot fill us'), and security is a condition for living well, never its source; good fortune (εὐτυχία) turns on a wheel.

types.name: Democracy: every wish governs
types.about: Every passing wish governs: each desire gets an equal vote, and the day is decided by whichever arrives first. Plato's democratic person lives from day to day, one day wine and music, the next a diet, then training, then idleness, then philosophy, with no order in life, and calls it freedom. Athena hears something else in ἐλευθερία, freedom: a word with ἔρως, love, inside it; and Athena warns that a 'democracy' in which desire holds the reins is already an oligarchic tyranny in disguise.

types.name: Tyranny: one desire governs
types.about: One desire governs: a craving, a fear, a person, a screen, a goal grown into an obsession, and the rest of the soul serves it. In Plato's last regime a single master passion takes the city of the soul, and the tyrant within is the least free of all, ruled by what rules him. Athena reads it psycho-politically: when the desiring part seizes the reins, the inner regime turns tyrannical. Yet desire, for Athena, is sacred in its motive: the soul is looking in one thing for the fullness of the Good.

items.prompt: You are offered a promotion: more money and a better title, but longer hours and less of what you love in the work. What decides it?

options.text: Whether it is good, for me and those around me, in the long run
options.note: You look at what is truly good over the years, for you and others.

options.text: The title: being recognised at last
options.note: Respect and standing in other people's eyes tip the balance.

options.text: The money, and the security it buys
options.note: Feeling safe and provided for is what tips the balance.

options.text: How I feel that morning; I'd change my mind twice
options.note: No single thing rules; the mood of the moment does.

options.text: Whether it leaves room for the one thing I can't stop wanting
options.note: One thing you cannot let go of decides it for everything else.

items.prompt: A Saturday with nothing planned. What usually decides how the day goes?

options.text: A few things I've chosen because they matter, done well
options.note: Your day follows what you have understood to be worthwhile.

options.text: Something that will show: progress, a goal, a win
options.note: You want the day to count, with something to point to by evening.

options.text: Chores, bills and errands that keep things safe and in order
options.note: Getting on top of things, so that you feel secure.

options.text: Whatever I feel like, one thing after another
options.note: Each wish takes its turn, and the day follows them.

options.text: The same place it always goes: the phone, a person, a craving, work
options.note: One pull keeps drawing the hours back to it.

items.prompt: Think of the last seven days. Share ten points among what really governed your choices.

options.text: What I understood to be right and good
Recognition: how I'd look, winning, being respected
Money, safety, keeping what I have
Whatever I wanted in the moment
One desire or worry that kept coming back

items.prompt: Quickly: which is more like you?

pairs.b: I spend on what I feel like

pairs.a: I know why I do what I do
pairs.b: I do it, then find the reasons

pairs.a: I can stop when I choose

items.prompt: When these pull against each other in you, which usually wins? Put them in order, the strongest first.

options.text: What I know is good
options.note: Your considered sense of what is right and worthwhile.

options.text: What earns respect
options.note: How it will look, and whether others will think well of you.

options.text: What keeps me safe and provided for
options.note: Money, savings, and keeping a cushion against hard times.

options.text: What I feel like right now
options.note: The wish of the moment, whatever it happens to be.

options.text: The one thing I can't stop wanting
options.note: A single craving, worry or person that keeps calling you back.

items.prompt: Describe one decision from this week, small or large. If you are honest, what really made it?
items.hint: A purchase, a yes you didn't mean, a message you sent, a night you stayed up.

items.prompt: If your soul were a city, what unwritten law does it actually live by? Write it as a law, even if you would never say it aloud.
items.hint: For example: “Never let them see you struggle”, “Always keep something in the bank”, “Whatever I feel, I do”.
items.placeholder: The law nobody wrote down is…

looks: What actually governs your choices: wisdom, honour, money and security, every passing wish, or one obsession.
learn: The five regimes of the Republic as states of the soul, and why you govern yourself first.

later.plan: Your own “constitution” for the week: three laws you give yourself, one «No» with its «Yes», and one act at your own scale.
later.shape: Maybe (not for every reflection): Add one practice with its dose; Cut one thing; Watch one cue; a check-in after 7 days (did you do it, what changed); a retake after 4 to 6 weeks.

ai: Read what actually governs the learner's choices as Plato's five regimes of the soul: wisdom (aristocracy), honour (timocracy), money and security (oligarchy), every passing wish (democracy), or one master desire (tyranny). Look at the pattern across the two scenarios, the points and the rank, then test it against the written decision and the unwritten law, which often show the real ruler more honestly than the scores. Read by Athena's psycho-politics: the polis mirrors the soul, justice is each part doing its own around the one Self, and when the desiring part seizes the reins the inner regime turns tyrannical, even while it calls itself freedom. Never moralise desire, money or ambition: for Athena desire is sacred in its motive, seeking the fullness of the Good, and security is a condition of living well, not its source. Quote the learner's own words, especially the unwritten law, and say which part of the soul wrote it. If the learner's charioteer result is there, compare it (the part that held the reins there is often the one on the throne here), and write an analysis only, with no plan or advice.
